Where the last millimeter of my drawing arm goes

My SO-101 arm draws a kitten with 1 mm of error. Here are the drawings, the controllers that made them better, and what still limits the arm: the pan joint.

Abstract

I want my SO-101 arm to put a tool exactly where I ask. To measure how close it gets, I make the arm draw on a tablet that records the pen tip. On four validation drawings, the physics controller from parts 3 and 4 misses by 2.74 mm. A correction that I learn from the planned path cuts this to 1.057 mm (Measured, real arm). The shoulder pan joint causes most of what is left. This part gives the setup, the controllers, the tests, and what I do not know yet.

Why draw on a tablet?

The goal. My arm will do kitting and carry tools. These are 3D motions with a payload that changes. The final controller can use only what the arm carries: joint encoders, and maybe a camera. So I want to know how accurate a cheap arm can be, which controller ideas make it better, and which physical effects set the limit.

The problem. The encoders measure joint angles. What I care about is where the tool tip goes. The two can differ: links bend, gears have play, and a pressed pen drags. At the pen, 1 mrad of pan angle is 0.231 mm, but an encoder cannot show a bend that happens after it. I need a judge outside the arm that measures the tip directly.

The idea. A tablet reports where a pen touches it. If the arm draws a path that I know exactly, the tablet tells me, moment by moment, how far the tip is from where it should be. The ink also shows the error to anyone (part 5).

What I measure. One number: the RMS distance between the pen tip and the reference path, over four validation drawings that never train anything. The tablet is a lab instrument. It gives the score, the labels for learning, and a way to find causes. The final controller must work without it. The datasheet gives an accuracy of ±0.25 mm at the center of the tablet. I have not finished checking it, so a difference below that is not proof.

The question: my arm draws with about 1 mm of error. Where does the rest come from, and which controller ideas reduced it?

Short on time? Read the picture below, watch the replay, and read the five findings. The rest of the page explains each finding, and the long parts are in closed drawers.

The drawing gets better with each change

Here is the whole story in one picture. It is the same kitten, drawn by the real arm with four controllers. Gray is the reference line. The colored line is where the pen really went, as measured by the tablet. The number is the error of the whole drawing: the root mean square (RMS) distance between the pen and the line, in millimeters. All four are Measured, which means the real arm drew them.

The top two drawings show the problem: the pen trails behind the line and wanders off it. The bottom two show what a learned correction does: the pen follows the line.

The other three validation drawings (a star, a spiral and a square that I made up) show the same pattern. Each column is one drawing: no correction on top, the frozen head below.

The setup, as a system

The arm holds a pen in the sleeve from part 5, and a Wacom Intuos tablet sits under the pen. The replay shows two real runs of the kitten, drawn again from the tablet recording. The second video shows the setup.

Input, output, and where the corrections happen

The diagram shows the whole system. The input is a drawing: a path in tablet millimeters. The output is where the pen tip really goes, read by the tablet. Blue boxes run in the final product. Orange boxes are lab only.

A correction can happen in three places.

  1. Inside the physics controller. It predicts the torque that the path needs and picks the best goal for the next 15 ticks. This is the physics base. A learned torque (PhysR) is one more correction here.
  2. On the path, before the controller (the correction head). It adds joint offsets that I learned from features of the planned path. The frozen head needs only the path, so it can run in the final product.
  3. From the tablet error (the online head). The head learns from the tablet while the arm draws. This needs the tablet, so it is a lab tool. I freeze the head before it is used.

The three letters on the diagram split the error: ccc is the correction, trtrtr is the servo lag, and uuu is what the encoders cannot see. The error budget below uses them.

Two words appear in every number.

  • Nib error. The distance between where the pen tip (the nib) should be and where the tablet says it is, at each moment. RMS averages it over a drawing: square each error, average, take the root. Errors of 1 mm and 3 mm give (12+32)/2=2.24\sqrt{(1^2 + 3^2)/2} = 2.24(12+32)/2​=2.24 mm. Big misses count more.
  • Validation drawings. Four drawings that never train anything.

What I found

  1. A learned correction does most of the work. Physics alone gives 2.74 mm. The frozen correction head gives 1.057 mm (Measured, mean of the four drawings).
  2. A better torque model alone cannot do it. Even a perfect servo, with zero tracking error, leaves 2.22 mm (Offline).
  3. The shoulder pan joint owns 61 % of the squared error of the uncorrected controller. It starts about 267 ms late after each direction change, and the pen lags the encoder reading on the same axis.
  4. Features beat bigger models. A neural network fits its training drawings to 0.85 mm and gains at most 0.02 mm on new drawings. Features that remember backlash and the last direction helped most (Offline).
  5. The pan dead band is friction, not backlash. The lag on the pen is still unexplained. Compliance is my leading suspect.

The controllers

Each controller sends a joint-angle goal to the servo at every tick. A tick is one step of the control loop, about 16.7 ms. The table says what each one does, which place in the diagram it changes, and what it needs while it draws. The results are in the chart above.

Name Where it acts What it does Needs while drawing
Physics base (phys) Controller Predicts 15 ticks ahead with a physical model of the arm and picks the best goal. An extended Kalman filter estimates a missing torque for each joint The encoder readings
PhysR Controller The physics base plus a small learned torque The encoder readings
Online correction head Head Adds a learned offset to the joint goals. It learns while the arm draws, from the tablet error The tablet
Frozen correction head Head The same head, with learning stopped The planned path only
Hysteresis models Head A correction learned from the planned path, with features for backlash and the last direction. Linear and kernel versions The planned path only
Neural-network correction Head A network that learns the correction, trained even on the exact test examples The planned path only
Fast Kalman head Head Follows the tablet error of the last few ticks The tablet
Whole-path planner (seqplan) Controller Plans the full drawing at once The path and a model

Where the error comes from

To find the causes, I remove one cause at a time and measure what is left. This is an error budget. It needs three parts that add up to the error eee. They are the three letters on the system diagram:

e=u+tr+ce = u + tr + c e=u+tr+c

  • trtrtr is tracking: where the encoders say the pen is, minus where I told it to go.
  • uuu is the gap the encoders cannot see (u for unseen): where the tablet says the pen is, minus where the encoders say. Anything that bends or slips after the encoder lands here.
  • ccc is the correction that a head adds. For the uncorrected controller, c=0c = 0c=0.

If tracking were perfect, tr=0tr = 0tr=0 and the error would be uuu alone: 2.22 mm. A torque model acts on tracking only, so this is its best case. It stops far above the 1.06 mm of the head.

The chart splits the squared error of the uncorrected controller into ten parts. They add up to 100 %.

Two bars are not arm errors. The tablet stream delay (about 20 ms) changes the score and not the ink. The unexplained rest holds tablet and encoder noise, about 0.4 mm. If the pan error were gone, the error would fall from 2.74 mm to 1.63 mm (Offline).

The numbers behind the budget

For the uncorrected controller, the mean of the four drawings gives (Measured, Offline fits):

e2=7.51 mm2=4.97⏟u2+1.69⏟tr2+0.85⏟cross term,e=7.51=2.74 mme^2 = 7.51\ \text{mm}^2 = \underbrace{4.97}_{u^2} + \underbrace{1.69}_{tr^2} + \underbrace{0.85}_{\text{cross term}}, \qquad e = \sqrt{7.51} = 2.74\ \text{mm} e2=7.51 mm2=u24.97​​+tr21.69​​+cross term0.85​​,e=7.51​=2.74 mm

The cross term exists because uuu and trtrtr are not independent.

A timing view shows the same story. If I shift the plan 115 ms earlier before I score, the error falls from 2.74 mm to 1.74 mm (Measured). At 20 mm/s, 115 ms is 2.3 mm of path. The frozen head learned this advance.

The pan axis

The pan is the joint at the base that turns the whole arm left and right. On my tablet it moves the pen mostly along x. One milliradian (mrad) of pan angle moves the pen 0.231 mm on x and 0.019 mm on y. The pan has two problems.

It starts late. The planner reverses a goal. The lift and the elbow follow within 50 ms. The pan follows 267 ms later (Measured, median of 46 events), then lags by about 10 mrad. At 0.231 mm per mrad, that is about 2.3 mm of pen.

The pen lags the encoders on x. The gap between the tablet and the encoders grows in a straight line with the pen speed along x. The slope is a lag of 86 ms on x and 35 ms on y. The encoders do not see this lag.

Why does the pan lag?

Three mechanical causes can make a joint lag. The table defines each one.

Suspect What it is What it predicts
Friction (stiction) The joint does not move until the servo torque beats a breakaway torque A dead zone around the goal, and a delay at a start from rest
Backlash A gap between gear teeth. The motor crosses the gap before the joint moves A fixed-angle gap at each reversal, whatever the torque
Compliance A part bends like a spring: deflection = torque ÷ stiffness. The base, the table or the pen holder can bend An error that grows with the torque. The encoders cannot see it

Friction explains the dead band. The servo torque is P×eP \times eP×e, where PPP is the servo gain register and eee is the position error. With friction, the joint moves only when PeP ePe beats the breakaway torque TTT, so the dead band is e=T/Pe = T / Pe=T/P. Doubling PPP halves it. A backlash gap is an angle that the gears fix, so doubling PPP does not change it. I held the pan at a goal at four values of PPP (Measured, direct holds from older logs):

PPP Pan dead band (mrad) Dead band times PPP
4 26.2 about 105
16 9.2 to 9.7 about 150
32 3.8 to 4.1 about 125
128 0.04 to 0.13 near zero, below one encoder tick

From PPP = 4 to 32, the product stays between 100 and 160. That is the signature of friction. Backlash in the loop is at most about 1 mrad. During drawing, the physics model removes part of the friction: the dead band is only 2.2 mrad, but the start after a pan reversal is still late.

Compliance is my leading suspect for the lag on x. The pan load reading (a percentage of maximum torque) predicts the x gap: −0.77-0.77−0.77 mm for each 10 % of load. With the load in the fit, the direction offset falls from −0.54-0.54−0.54 to −0.14-0.14−0.14 mm (Offline fit on Measured logs). A fixed gap would not follow the torque. The encoders cannot see play or bending outside the servo, so a PPP test cannot test it.

Pen drag is a fourth suspect. A pressed pen drags against the motion. The direction offset on x grows with press depth, from −0.44 mm at 0.5 mm press to −1.01 mm at 2.0 mm. It is zero on y and about zero in hover. But 32 to 36 ms of the x lag stays in hover, so drag is not the whole story. I have not run the hover replay that would decide it.

What worked

A correction learned from the planned path

The physics base is wrong in a repeatable way. 98 % of its error repeats from run to run (2.58 mm repeatable, 0.58 mm random). An error that repeats can be learned.

The correction head is a linear map from features of the planned motion to five joint-angle offsets. The features are the sine, cosine, angle, speed, acceleration and a saturated speed of each joint: 30 numbers plus a constant. The head learns online with recursive least squares (RLS): after each tick, it adjusts its weights to shrink the error that the tablet just reported.

The features do the work. I ran the same head with fewer features (Measured):

Head Validation mean (mm)
No head 2.74
Constant offsets only 2.64
Pose features only 2.65
All features 1.03

The online head needs the tablet while it draws. So I freeze it: the weights stay, learning stops, and the head needs only the planned path. The frozen head scores 1.057 mm in the control block of my A B A test. That is the best controller that I measured.

The math of the RLS head

Call the feature vector ϕk\phi_kϕk​, with the constant appended (31 numbers), and the weights WWW (5 × 31 = 155 numbers). The head outputs the joint offsets

gk=Wϕkg_k = W \phi_k gk​=Wϕk​

When the tablet error arrives, convert it to a joint-space label yky_kyk​ (the offset that would have cancelled it, through the nib Jacobian). RLS then runs three steps:

Kk=Pk−1ϕkλ+ϕk⊤Pk−1ϕk,Wk=Wk−1+(yk−Wk−1ϕk) Kk⊤,Pk=1λ(Pk−1−Kkϕk⊤Pk−1)K_k = \frac{P_{k-1}\phi_k}{\lambda + \phi_k^\top P_{k-1}\phi_k}, \qquad W_k = W_{k-1} + (y_k - W_{k-1}\phi_k)\,K_k^\top, \qquad P_k = \frac{1}{\lambda}\left(P_{k-1} - K_k \phi_k^\top P_{k-1}\right) Kk​=λ+ϕk⊤​Pk−1​ϕk​Pk−1​ϕk​​,Wk​=Wk−1​+(yk​−Wk−1​ϕk​)Kk⊤​,Pk​=λ1​(Pk−1​−Kk​ϕk⊤​Pk−1​)

PPP is the inverse of the data matrix. It is the filter's memory of how sure it is, and it shrinks as data comes in. The forgetting factor λ≤1\lambda \le 1λ≤1 weighs old data. With λ=1\lambda = 1λ=1, nothing is forgotten. In my deployed code, a cap on PPP binds on 96 % of the updates, so λ=0.999\lambda = 0.999λ=0.999 does almost nothing (tested with real features and synthetic labels).

Hysteresis features

The first fork-and-flush round found that the winning features are hysteresis features. Hysteresis means that the output depends on the history of the input. A gear with a gap has it: the joint position depends on which way the motor came from. A play operator is a tiny model of a gap. It keeps a state sss that stays still while the input qqq moves inside a gap of width www, and follows when the input pushes against an edge:

sk=min⁡ ⁣(max⁡(sk−1, qk−w/2), qk+w/2)s_k = \min\!\big(\max(s_{k-1},\, q_k - w/2),\ q_k + w/2\big) sk​=min(max(sk−1​,qk​−w/2), qk​+w/2)

Play operators of several widths, plus the sign of the last motion, give the correction a memory of the backlash state of each joint. I use the word for the features, not as a proven cause: the unexplained part of the gap has the same size when a joint stands still and when it moves.

I did not find these features myself. I used fork-and-flush auto research (Cai et al., Microsoft Research): a lead starts several agents from the same workspace state, each with a fresh context. A frozen scorer that the agents cannot edit scores them. The lead continues from the winner. The dev motions chose the models. The sealed motions are four drawings that nobody used until the end.

Model Dev score (mm) Sealed score (mm)
Old linear model (30 features) 1.1766 1.1314
Linear hysteresis model 1.0341 1.0285
Kernel model 0.9852 1.0077

All Offline. The kernel adds only 0.02 mm over the linear model on the sealed motions. The gain comes from the features, not from the model class.

The rules of my fork-and-flush runs

I fixed these rules before round 1.

  1. Each round has three forks, each running for 45 to 50 minutes.
  2. The winner is the lowest score of the frozen scorer on the dev motions. I do not use the number that a fork reports.
  3. A new round starts from the winner only if it gains 0.02 mm or more.
  4. The sealed motions are scored once, on the final winner, after a check that no fork read them.
  5. A candidate gets an arm slot only if it gains 0.05 mm or more on both dev and sealed.
  6. The arm test is A B A against the frozen head, with the 0.12 mm threshold.

Round 2 gained 0.005 mm, so the run stopped after two rounds. My prediction before round 1 was 1.10 to 1.14 mm. The result was 0.99 mm. I was too pessimistic. About 35 dev scores chose the details, so dev differences below 0.01 mm are noise.

What did not work

Idea What I did Result
A bigger neural network Trained it even on the exact test motions 0.847 mm on those motions, but only 0.022 mm better than a ridge (a linear fit with a penalty on big weights) on new ones: 1.025 against 1.047 mm (Offline). On the arm, two network corrections measured 1.14 to 1.15 mm, worse than the frozen head (Measured)
A better torque model alone A better phys, PhysR or a torque network Stops at 2.22 mm in the best case. PhysR measured 2.27 mm
Whole-path planning (seqplan) Plan the entire drawing ahead, not 15 ticks At most 5 % better on the exact model. With a small model error, 23 % to 364 % worse (Simulation). I recommend dropping it
A fast Kalman head Follow the tablet error of the last ~5 ticks 0.74 to 0.84 mm (Offline), a big gain. But it reads the tablet while it draws, so it is a lab tool. Tuned for no lag, it diverges to 4 to 6 mm if the real lag is 30 ms or more
A new shoulder lift servo Swap one servo Lift tracking owns 0 to 2 % of the error. Dropped

Why does the network fail? The error that is left on a repeated motion, about 0.5 to 0.6 mm, is specific to that motion. No feature that I tried predicts it on a new motion: the held-out R2R^2R2 is at most 0. A network cannot learn a pattern that the inputs do not contain. Whole-path planning fails because the model error grows with the horizon: 0.40 mm at 1 tick and 1.81 mm at 10 ticks. A plan built on that model inherits the error.

How much data does a correction need?

A learning curve retrains each model on 3, 6, 9 and 12 distinct motions and scores held-out motions (Offline).

Distinct motions beat repeats. Twelve motions with one run each (12 runs) give 1.039 mm. Six motions with 17.6 runs in total give 1.067 mm. The 12 distinct motions win with fewer runs. New arm time is best spent on new drawings: 12 new scribbles take about 27 minutes.

The tests I use

Each test answers one question and guards against one way to fool myself.

Test The question How it works
Error budget Which cause owns how much error? Split eee into parts that add up, then remove one at a time
A B A ordering Is the new controller really better? Run baseline A, new B, baseline A. The same controller drifts by 0.12 mm in an hour (1.03 then 1.14 mm), so B must win by more than that
Sealed set Did I tune to my own score? Four motions that nobody sees until one final look
Learning curve Do I need more data? Retrain on 3, 6, 9, 12 motions and extrapolate
Press sweep Is the pen drag a cause? Same motions at four press depths

The A B A test for the new hysteresis models on the arm has not run. My stack test started at 01:04, and the arm computer went offline at about 01:30 with the battery dead.

Where this can be wrong

  • Offline is not the arm. The Offline scorer treats the uncorrected error as independent of the correction. On the frozen-head runs, it predicts the new linear model at 1.24 mm, while the frozen head measured 1.06 mm. Part 4 showed the same gap. The hysteresis numbers are candidates.
  • The tablet is the judge. The datasheet accuracy is ±0.25 mm at the center, so differences below that are weak evidence. Its stream arrives about 20 ms late. I estimated this from three indirect methods that agree within 10 to 30 ms. There is no hardware sync. Tablet noise is about 0.4 mm.
  • The validation set is small. Four drawings, and a test-retest drift of 0.12 mm.
  • The cause of the pan lag on x is unknown. Friction explains the dead band, not the 86 ms lag. The project notes say that the servo encoder sits on the output shaft, so backlash inside the servo is at most about 1 mrad. I did not verify this against a datasheet. The late start is 267 ms in one count and 235 ms in another, so I quote about 250 ms.
  • The drag cause is only supported. The hover replay did not run.
  • One arm, one tablet pose. The pan result may change at another tablet place. The 24 and 48 motion values are extrapolations.

Check yourself

Each question gives all the facts it needs. Pick an answer, then open the reasoning.

Question 1. A physics controller draws with an error of 2.74 mm. With perfect servo tracking it would be 2.22 mm. A friend says a better torque network will reach 1.0 mm. What do you reply?

  • A. "Yes, a better network models the servo perfectly, so it reaches zero." This forgets the gap uuu.
  • B. "No. A torque model acts on tracking only, and perfect tracking still leaves 2.22 mm." This uses the budget.
  • C. "Maybe. The score has 0.12 mm of noise, so 1.0 is close to 2.22." The noise is far too small to close a 1.2 mm gap.
Answer

B. With tr=0tr = 0tr=0, the error is u=2.22u = 2.22u=2.22 mm. The encoders cannot see uuu, and a torque model acts only on tracking.

Question 2. A controller measures 1.057 mm. An hour later, the same controller measures 1.14 mm on the same drawings. A new controller scores 1.00 mm in one run. Is it better?

  • A. "Yes. 1.00 is below 1.057." The gain, 0.057 mm, is smaller than the 0.08 mm that the same controller moved on its own.
  • B. "Not shown. Run baseline, new, baseline and compare." This puts the drift on both sides of the new run.
  • C. "No. The second baseline was 1.14, so the new one is worse." The new controller is 1.00, not 1.14.
Answer

B. One run of each cannot beat the drift. A B A can. In my notes the threshold is 0.12 mm.

Question 3. A servo makes torque P×eP \times eP×e. A joint with stiction starts to move only when this torque beats a breakaway torque TTT. A second joint has a backlash gap of 3 mrad. You double PPP. What happens?

  • A. "Both halve, because a larger PPP tightens everything." A gap is a geometry and does not depend on PPP.
  • B. "The stiction dead zone T/PT/PT/P halves. The backlash gap stays at 3 mrad." This follows from the formulas.
  • C. "Neither changes. PPP only changes the speed." PPP sets the torque for a given error, so it moves the dead zone.
Answer

B. This is why the dead band table above points to friction. A real joint can have both, so the drop is then partial.

What I test next

Each test has a prediction.

  1. A drawing block at PPP = 16, 32, 16 on the pan (A B A). It is running as I write. Rule: PPP = 32 wins if it lowers the error by 0.12 mm or more. Earlier circles at PPP = 32 had 6 to 12 % less total error than at PPP = 16. Prediction: the gain is small, because the physics model already removes most of the friction effect.
  2. The hover replay and a low-friction nib. Prediction: the direction offset on x falls to about zero in hover.
  3. A speed sweep at 10, 20 and 40 mm/s. Prediction: it splits the 86 ms lag from the −0.54 mm offset.
  4. The hysteresis models on the arm, A B A against the frozen head. Prediction: a frozen model scores 1.05 to 1.15 mm, so it does not beat the frozen head by 0.12 mm. I give this a 65 % chance. An online head with the same features is the stronger candidate.
  5. New distinct scribbles, and ILC on one repeated drawing. Prediction: 27 minutes of arm time for 12 new motions lowers the held-out error more than the same time on repeats. I expect ILC (iterative learning control, which corrects the next run of a path from the last error) to reach about 0.6 to 0.7 mm. It is a same-path reference, not a proof of a bound.

I keep the rule from part 4: I choose models by their closed-loop error on the real arm.
